title: [D4 Policy] Composition rule engine — scope before severity
summary: `helena.policy` is the sixth versioned package and `helena.policy.v1` is the composition rule, frozen the moment an assessment records `policy_version = "v1"` — the version dimension that had no owner until now. `constrain(result, supports)` takes a model's verdict and the cited evidence fused with the per-entity traffic (`supports_for(result, projection)`) and returns a `Decision`: permitted, or constrained with every rule that fired named and the two limitations the rule cannot test recorded as first-class policy gaps. It never rewrites the `AgentResult`, and it is enforced after the prompt rather than inside it.
assumption_validated: That `concept/02`'s composition rule can be written as deterministic policy over what the store already holds, rather than as prompt wording. It can, for six of its seven sentences: the traffic tests (bidirectional bytes, contacted-as-flow-destination, port_matched) and the taxonomy tests (contact paths vs host-state paths, the address/domain scope split) are all decidable from a `ContextProjection` plus an `AgentResult`, and each is a table row that fails when the rule is mutated (three mutations checked). The seventh — shared infrastructure — is only partly decidable: a resolver is observable from the ports the host reached, and CDN / cloud tenant / shared subdomain are external facts no source in this deployment supplies. That is a NEGATIVE result and it is recorded as a policy outcome (`shared_infrastructure_undetermined`) on every `malicious` verdict the missing test let through, rather than approximated. A second negative: the evidence taxonomy is roots-only in v1, so no rule can key on 'this is a phishing indicator'; the phishing sentence is encoded through the proposed CONTEXT path instead (contact reaches `malicious.phishing`, never `malicious.compromised`), which is what makes it work at all.
makes_buildable: Task 33's escalation evaluator gets three things: `helena.policy.Support` is the (claim + per-entity traffic) record its step 1 needs, `policy.v1.constrain` is its step 3 ('a hit whose traffic does not support it does not escalate as `malicious`') already written and tested, and `policy_version` now names a real module so 'record the policy version on every assessment' has something to record. Its own additions are the per-source confidence thresholds in a versioned policy file, the aggregator rule, and the read over the store rather than over a result — deliberately not here, because the escalation input must be independent of the model's answer and this reads one. D5 storage gets a `Decision` to store beside the assessment; D6 orchestration gets the two-line call (`supports_for` then `constrain`) and owns what to do with `permits = None`.

verification.detail: 1094 passed in 265.63 s, no skips, against the pinned engine (`source bin/env.sh` first). 37 of them are the new tests/test_policy.py: 15 table rows (one per rule plus the permitted case each rule is the negation of), the coverage tests that fail if a rule or a gap kind has no row, the constant-equality test between `policy.v1.FLOW_DESTINATION` and `rendering.OBSERVATION_LAYERS`, and 4 integration tests that build a real context from the committed capture, load the committed ThreatFox extract, and decide over the view's own `port_matched` rather than over a fixture's idea of it. Three mutations checked and each failed the suite: dropping `observed_bytes_received > 0` from the bidirectional predicate (1 failure), turning the shared-infrastructure rule's `all` into `any` so a corroborating support stopped corroborating (1 failure), and dropping the `domain_scope_untestable` gap from the domain rule (2 failures).

escalations.detail: The policy's two gaps (`domain_scope_untestable`, `shared_infrastructure_undetermined`) are its own vocabulary and are NOT `helena.contracts.v1.GAP_KINDS`. None of the contract's seven kinds names 'a test that does not apply'; `missing` is the tempting one and spelling it would collapse 'the lookup did not happen' into 'the rule could not be run', which `concept/instruction.md` §2 forbids at every layer. Attaching one of these to an `AgentResult` — so a stored assessment carries it beside the model's own gaps — needs either a contract `v2` with an eighth gap kind or an explicit decision to reuse one of the seven, and adding a gap kind is a change to the agent contract (`concept/instruction.md` §3). Not blocking: the gaps live on the `Decision`, which is the record D5 will store beside the assessment anyway. ADR-0022 §5.

Three of `concept/02`'s four shared-infrastructure cases — CDN, cloud tenant, shared subdomain — are external facts about an address or a name, and nothing in this repository supplies one. Ruled out before writing, not after: `helena.enrichment.SOURCES` has two feeds and neither says so; the Public Suffix List is deliberately unregistered and `helena/enrichment.py` says it 'makes no claim about any entity, and it can neither escalate nor suppress', so using its private section to withhold severity would break that statement; Netify is Tier D and 'never a threat classification or a decision about an entity' (ADR-0009) and is not loaded at all. Settling it needs a source that declares infrastructure roles, which is a governed decision (`concept/05`) and not a session's. ADR-0022 §6.

deferred: STORING A DECISION. No assessment table exists (task 26 deferred it to D5), so the `Decision`, its findings and its gaps are typed and countable in memory and in nothing else. `concept/instruction.md` §7's 'every new failure path is typed, stored and countable' stays open for the agent and policy layers exactly as tasks 26-31 left it. What D5 should count here is constrained-versus-permitted per rule: a rule that never fires is a rule that is wrong or a rule nothing reaches, and both are worth knowing before the thresholds are argued about.

CALLING IT. Nothing invokes `constrain` in a pipeline: `helena.triage.run` returns the model's answer and stops, and building the pair (a projection plus the result of a run over it) is D6 orchestration's. Wiring it into the triage runner was considered and rejected — the runner's job is one model call, the policy reads a projection the runner is not given, and a runner that read the store would be the triage stage acquiring a second input beside 'a bounded rendering, and nothing else'.

ROUTING ON `permits = None`. The policy refuses to turn 'this evidence establishes nothing' into a verdict, because both available answers (`normal`, `unknown`) would be a claim the evidence does not carry. What a router does with it is D6's, and it needs the escalation evaluator beside it to be a safe decision at all.

THE ALL-`no_match` `normal`. The failure mode the `normal` rule is named for — reading a context of nothing but `no_match` as a clean bill of health — is not visible from citations, because a `no_match` carries no evidence identifier to cite. The rule catches the half that is visible (a `normal` whose cited support is entirely evidence-level `normal`/`no_match`); catching the other half needs a read over the store, which is task 33's shape. ADR-0022 §4.

PER-SOURCE THRESHOLDS AND A POLICY CONFIGURATION FILE. Task 33's step, and deliberately not anticipated here: this version has no numeric threshold at all except `bytes > 0`, which is `concept/02`'s own wording ('no bytes returned'). A `config/policy.toml` written now would be a file with one value nobody had measured.
lessons: task 32: THE COMPOSITION RULE CANNOT KEY ON THE EVIDENCE'S THREAT TYPE, BECAUSE THE EVIDENCE TAXONOMY IS ROOTS-ONLY. `helena/taxonomy/v1.py` closes the evidence level over five roots and no children — deliberately, because concept/02 adopts that vocabulary from a published taxonomy it neither names nor reproduces — so a ThreatFox hit is `malicious` and never `malicious.c2`. 'A C2 hit' and 'a phishing domain' are therefore not readable from a claim. What works instead is keying on the PROPOSED CONTEXT PATH: concept/02's malicious family splits into contact (`c2`, `payload`, `phishing`) and host state (`compromised`, `hostile`, `spam`, `exfiltration`), and the phishing sentence becomes 'contact reaches `malicious.phishing` and never `malicious.compromised`'. Any later increment that wants a rule per threat type needs a taxonomy v2 first.

task 32: `port_matched` IS THE ONE PIECE OF SCOPE-BEFORE-SEVERITY THAT IS ALREADY IN THE STORE AND WAS WAITING FOR THIS TASK. sql/migrations/0015 computes it three-valued and explicitly does not filter on it, with a comment saying that filtering would be 'the view making the composition rule's decision'. `a_port_scoped_claim_needs_the_port_the_host_reached` is that decision, and it is the one rule here that is exercised end to end over real feed rows — 3 375 of the ThreatFox snapshot's records are `ip:port`, so it is also the common case rather than the corner one.

task 32: THE POLICY MUST NOT REWRITE THE `AgentResult`, AND THE REASON IS EVALUATION RATHER THAN PURITY. `concept/07` appends inference and never overwrites a fact; the operational consequence is that an evaluation which could not tell a model's answer from a policy's correction of it would be scoring the policy while reporting on the model. So `constrain` returns a separate `Decision` carrying `proposed` and `permits` side by side, and nothing mutates a result.

task 32: A CAP IS A BARE ROOT, NEVER A PATH, AND IT IS RESOLVED THROUGH `taxonomy.for_emission` FOR THE RESULT'S OWN EMITTER. concept/02's 'emit the parent rather than guessing a child' applies one level up: naming which kind of `suspicious` a capped verdict is would be inventing the reason. Putting the cap through the taxonomy is what stops a future rule capping to something the emitter could not have said.

task 32: `permits` HAS TO BE THREE-VALUED. Two of the seven rules say the evidence establishes NOTHING (concept/02's word for shared infrastructure is 'transfers nothing', and `normal` on contacted indicators 'never establishes normal on its own'), and there is no weaker verdict to cap to — `normal` would be the claim the rule just refused and `unknown` means unassessable, which is a different fact. `None` is the honest third value and turning it into a verdict is left to whatever routes on it.

task 32: `unknown` IS OFF THE SEVERITY SCALE AND THAT HAS TO BE STRUCTURAL. `SEVERITY` holds `normal`/`suspicious`/`malicious` only and no rule has a precondition that fires on `unknown`, so an unassessable verdict passes through unconstrained. A scale with `unknown` on it would let a cap silently turn 'the run established nothing' into a graded verdict, which is the collapse concept/02 spends a paragraph forbidding.

task 32: A TABLE-DRIVEN RULE SUITE NEEDS A COVERAGE TEST OVER THE TABLE, NOT JUST THE ROWS. `test_every_rule_has_a_case_in_the_table` and `test_every_gap_kind_has_a_case_in_the_table` compare the set of rules the table exercises against `RULES` and `GAP_KINDS`, so a later version that adds a rule and forgets a row fails here rather than shipping untested policy. Each row also states the WHOLE answer (outcome, permits, rules fired, gaps) — a row asserting only the outcome passes while the decision names the wrong rule.

task 32: LOADING A FEED FIXTURE `now - 1 minute` PRODUCES NO CLAIM AT ALL FOR A RE-STAMPED CAPTURE, SILENTLY. The enriched context joins the snapshot valid at `window_start`, and a window that started up to five minutes ago is BEFORE a load one minute ago, so `window_start >= valid_from` fails and the entity renders with no claim. Load at `datetime.fromtimestamp(current_window())` — the window's own start — which is task 25's rule reaching a third test module.
failed_approaches: task 32: Using the Public Suffix List's private section to identify shared infrastructure (`*.workers.dev`, `blogspot.com`, `s3.amazonaws.com` — the section exists precisely to list suffixes under which unrelated parties register names). Resolved before it was written: `helena/enrichment.py` states that the PSL 'makes no claim about any entity, and it can neither escalate nor suppress', and using it to withhold a malicious verdict is using it to suppress. It is also not in the projection, so it would have needed a new query or a migration to reach the rule at all.

task 32: Using Netify's category to identify a CDN or a cloud tenant. ADR-0009 makes it Tier D supplying 'application identity and category and never a threat classification or a decision about an entity'; withholding severity on its say-so is a decision about an entity. It is also not registered in `helena.enrichment.SOURCES` and nothing loads it.

task 32: Minting a `helena.contracts.v1.Gap(kind=MISSING, ...)` for the domain-scope limitation so the honest limitation could ride on the `AgentResult`. `missing` means the lookup did not happen; the domain case is a lookup that succeeded and a scope test that does not apply. Collapsing the two is what `concept/instruction.md` §2 forbids at every layer, and the contract's seven kinds are frozen — so the policy carries its own two kinds and the contract question is escalated instead.

task 32: Keying `contact_is_not_compromise` on the evidence's threat type (`native_evidence->>'threat_type'` carries ThreatFox's `botnet_cc`, `phishing` and so on). It would work only for ThreatFox: the evidence taxonomy is roots-only, so the rule would be reading one publisher's format in a frozen policy module — the loader/view line task 23 recorded, crossed in the other direction. The rule keys on the proposed context path instead, which is version-frozen vocabulary and the same for every feed.

task 32: Making the composition rule part of `helena.triage.run`. Rejected before it was written: the runner is given 'a bounded rendering, and nothing else' and the policy reads a `ContextProjection`, so wiring it in would have made the triage stage read the store. The pair is assembled by whatever holds both, which is D6 orchestration.
next_session_should_know: Task 33 is the deterministic escalation evaluator and this task built half its input. SIX THINGS TO CARRY. (1) THE CALL IS TWO LINES: `supports = policy.supports_for(result, projection)` then `policy.version('v1').constrain(result, supports)`. `constrain` raises `PolicyError` for the two things that are the caller's fault — a result recording another `policy_version`, and a support list that is not exactly the result's citations — and returns a `Decision` otherwise. It never raises for a verdict it disagrees with; disagreement is the return value. (2) YOUR EVALUATOR MUST NOT READ A `Decision` OR AN `AgentResult`. `concept/04` makes deterministic escalation independent of whether triage ran at all, and `helena.triage.escalates` is already the triage half. What you share with this module is `Support` — the (claim + per-entity traffic) record — which you will have to build from the projection directly rather than from citations, because you are asking about every claim in the context and not about the ones a model chose to cite. Consider adding a second constructor beside `supports_for` rather than reusing it; the resolution loop is six lines. (3) STEP 3 OF YOUR TASK IS ALREADY WRITTEN. 'Apply the composition rule so a hit whose traffic does not support it does not escalate as malicious' is `_contacted_with_traffic_both_ways` plus `_port_not_reached`'s condition; call `constrain` on a synthesised `malicious` verdict, or lift the predicates — but if you lift them, note that they are frozen in `v1` and a copy is a second copy. (4) `policy_version` NOW NAMES A REAL MODULE. Test fixtures across the suite still use placeholders (`'pol1'` in tests/test_agents.py, tests/test_triage.py, tests/test_contracts.py); anything that will actually reach `constrain` must record `helena.policy.v1.POLICY_VERSION`. Your per-source thresholds file is the second thing `policy_version` will cover, and putting it in `config/policy.toml` beside `config/rendering.toml` and `config/hosts.toml` is the shape ADR-0019 established for policy that is a location rather than an environment variable. (5) THE SHARED-INFRASTRUCTURE TEST IS ONE CASE OUT OF FOUR AND THE ABSENCE IS RECORDED, NOT HIDDEN. Every permitted `malicious` decision carries `shared_infrastructure_undetermined`. If your escalation path establishes `malicious` on a Tier A hit, it inherits that gap — do not let a green suite read as a tested CDN rule. (6) THE FULL SUITE IS NOW 1 094 TESTS IN ~266 s ON THIS MACHINE, WITH NO SKIPS. Budget against that; it is faster than the ~480 s task 28 recorded because the engine was already up.
